title: E2 on a cyclohexane ring: which alkene forms
asks: A substituted cyclohexyl halide meets a strong base. Circle the major elimination product.

know.h: {{E2}} needs the hydrogen and the leaving group anti-periplanar: on neighbouring carbons, in one plane, pointing in opposite directions. The lecture calls this the most important factor for {{E2}}.
On a chair, anti-periplanar means trans-diaxial: the leaving group axial, and an axial hydrogen on the next carbon. Neighbouring axial bonds point opposite ways, one up and one down.
An equatorial leaving group cannot react. What lies anti to an equatorial bond is a ring C-C bond, never a hydrogen. (The lecture's Newman projection shows an equatorial group anti to a ring carbon.)
The ring flip turns every axial group equatorial and every equatorial group axial. Up stays up and down stays down, so cis and trans do not change.
The chair that reacts is the one with the leaving group axial, even when it is the less stable chair. If it is the less stable chair, the reaction is slower but it still goes through that chair.

Reading a wedge and dash drawing as a chair. Axial bonds alternate up, down, up, down around the ring. So if an up group is axial on C1, an up group on C2 is equatorial and a down group on C2 is axial.
Cis neighbour (leaving group and R on the same face of C1 and C2): with the leaving group axial, R is equatorial, so C2 has an axial hydrogen. The double bond can form toward R.
Trans neighbour (opposite faces): with the leaving group axial, R is axial too, so the hydrogen on C2 is equatorial and cannot leave. The double bond must form on the other side, away from R.
Saytzeff (Zaitsev) rule: when two different axial hydrogens are available, the more substituted alkene is the major product. Geometry is checked first, the rule second.

A tert-butyl group locks the ring. Axial tert-butyl costs 5.5 kcal/mol (K = 11,916), so the chair with tert-butyl equatorial is the only one that matters. The other groups are then fixed as axial or equatorial by being cis or trans to it.
Carbons that are not part of the reaction keep their configuration. A substituent on a wedge stays on a wedge unless its carbon becomes part of the C=C.
Strong base plus a secondary ring halide or tosylate gives mostly {{E2}}. Cl, Br, I and {{OTs}} are all leaving groups that work. The ether from substitution is at most a minor product.
Only hydrogens on the two ring carbons next to the leaving group count. Hydrogens on a methyl substituent on C2 are one carbon too far away.

method: Confirm it is E2: a strong base and a leaving group on a ring carbon.
Number the ring from the carbon with the leaving group, and note whether each substituent is up (wedge) or down (dash).
Draw the chair in which the leaving group is axial, and work out whether each other group is axial or equatorial in that chair.
Look at the two neighbouring carbons. Each one has an axial position pointing away from the leaving group: does it hold a hydrogen or a substituent?
Every axial hydrogen found gives one alkene, with the double bond between its carbon and the leaving-group carbon. With two choices, the more substituted alkene is major.
Draw the product: remove that hydrogen and the leaving group, and keep every other group on its original wedge or dash.

pitfalls.h: Circling the Zaitsev alkene without checking that its hydrogen can be anti to the leaving group.
Working from the more stable chair when the leaving group is equatorial in it. That chair does not react.
Removing an equatorial hydrogen. An equatorial hydrogen is gauche to an axial leaving group, not anti.
Changing the wedge or dash of a carbon that takes no part in the reaction.
Choosing the substitution product when the question asks for the elimination product.
Thinking the ring flip can turn a trans pair into a cis pair. It cannot: only axial and equatorial change.
